{{Short description|Theorem in arithmetic combinatorics}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
In [[arithmetic combinatorics]], the '''Erdős–Szemerédi theorem''' states that for every [[finite set]] <math>A</math> of [[integer]]s, at least one of the sets <math>A+A</math> and <math>A\cdot A</math> (the sets of [[Sumset|pairwise sums]] and pairwise products, respectively) form a significantly larger set. More precisely, the Erdős–Szemerédi theorem states that there exist positive constants <math>c</math> and <math>\varepsilon</math> such that, for any non-empty set <math>A\subset\N</math>,

<math display="block">\max( |A+A|, |A \cdot A| ) \geq c |A|^{1+\varepsilon}.</math>

It was proved by [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Endre Szemerédi]] in 1983.<ref name=":0">{{citation
 | last1 = Erdős | first1 = Paul | author1-link = Paul Erdős
 | last2 = Szemerédi | first2 = Endre | author2-link = Endre Szemerédi
 | chapter = On sums and products of integers
 | location = Basel
 | mr = 820223
 | pages = 213–218
 | publisher = Birkhäuser Verlag
 | title = Studies in Pure Mathematics. To the memory of Paul Turán
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-0348-5438-2_19
 | isbn = 978-3-7643-1288-6
 | year = 1983}}.</ref>  The notation <math>|A|</math> denotes the [[cardinality]] of the set <math>A</math>.

The set of pairwise sums is <math>A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}</math> and is called the [[sumset]] of <math>A</math>.

The set of pairwise products is <math>A\cdot A=\{a\cdot b:a,b\in A\}</math> and is called the product set of <math>A</math>; it is also written <math>AA</math>.

The theorem is a version of the maxim that additive structure and multiplicative structure cannot coexist. It can also be viewed as an assertion that the [[Number line|real line]] does not contain any set resembling a finite [[subring]] or finite [[Subfield (mathematics)|subfield]]; it is the first example of what is now known as the '''sum-product phenomenon''', which is now known to hold in a wide variety of rings and fields, including finite fields.<ref>{{citation|last=Tao|first=Terence|title=The sum-product phenomenon in arbitrary rings|journal=Contributions to Discrete Mathematics|volume=4|issue=2|pages=59–82|arxiv=0806.2497|doi=10.11575/cdm.v4i2.61994|doi-access=free|bibcode=2008arXiv0806.2497T|mr=2592424|author-link=Terence Tao|date=2009 |hdl=10515/sy5r78637}}.</ref>

== Sum-product conjecture ==
The sum-product conjecture informally says that one of the sum set or the product set of any set must be nearly as large as possible. It was originally conjectured by Erdős in 1974 to hold whether <math>A</math> is a set of integers, reals, or complex numbers.<ref>{{citation |first=P. |last=Erdős |contribution=Some recent problems and results in graph theory, combinatorics and number theory |title=Proceedings of the Seventh Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and Computing, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana |year=1976 |pages=3–14 |series=Utilitas Mathematica |location=Winnipeg, Manitoba |mr=0422031|zbl=352.05024}}</ref> More precisely, it proposes that, for any set <math>A\subset\C</math>, one has

<math display="block">\max(|A+A|,|A \cdot A|) \geq |A|^{2-o(1)}.</math>

The asymptotic parameter in the <math>o(1)</math> [[little o notation]] is <math>|A|</math>.

=== Disproving the conjecture ===
This conjecture was disproved over the reals (and hence the complex numbers) in 2026 by Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut, and Zhelezov,<ref name="BSSZ2026">{{cite arXiv|last1=Bloom |first1=Thomas F. |last2=Sawin |first2=Will |last3=Schildkraut |first3=Carl |last4=Zhelezov |first4=Dmitrii |title=The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers |date=2026-05-27  |class=math.NT |eprint=2605.28781 }}</ref> who constructed arbitrarily large sets <math>A\subset R</math> of [[algebraic integer]]s in [[algebraic number field|number fields]] of degree proportional to <math>\log|A|</math> such that

<math display="block">\max(|A+A|,|A \cdot A|) \leq |A|^{2-c}</math>

for an absolute constant <math>c>0</math>. The same paper disproves the ''many sums and products conjecture'' and obtains analogous constructions over [[p-adic number|{{mvar|p}}-adic numbers]], [[finite field]]s, and [[Algebraic function field|function fields]] in positive characteristic. The conjecture remains open over the integers.

== Examples ==
If <math>A=\{1,2,3,\dots,n\}</math>, then <math>|A+A|=2|A|-1\O(|A|)</math> using [[Big O notation]], with <math>|A|</math> the asymptotic parameter. Informally, this says that the sum set of <math>A</math> grows only proportionally to <math>A</math>. On the other hand, the product set of <math>A</math> satisfies a bound of the form <math>|A\cdot A|\ge|A|^{2-\varepsilon}</math> for all <math>\varepsilon>0</math> and all sufficiently large <math>n</math>. This is related to the Erdős [[multiplication table]] problem.<ref>{{citation|first=Paul|last=Erdős|author-link=Paul Erdős|title=An asymptotic inequality in the theory of numbers|journal=Vestnik Leningradskogo Universiteta |volume=15|year=1960|pages=41–49|mr=0126424}}</ref> The best lower bound on <math>|A\cdot A|</math> for this set is due to [[Kevin Ford (mathematician)|Kevin Ford]].<ref>{{Citation|last=Ford|first=Kevin|chapter=Sums and Products from a Finite Set of Real Numbers|date=1998|title=Analytic and Elementary Number Theory|series=Developments in Mathematics|volume=1|pages=59–66|place=Boston, Massachusetts|publisher=Springer US|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-4507-8_7|isbn=978-1-4419-5058-1|s2cid=117873720 }}</ref>

This example is an instance of the ''few sums, many products''<ref name=":2">{{citation|last1=Elekes |first1=György|author1-link=György Elekes|last2=Ruzsa|first2=Imre Z.|author2-link=Imre Z. Ruzsa|date=2003-08-01|title=Few sums, many products|journal=Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica|volume=40|issue=3|pages=301–308|doi=10.1556/sscmath.40.2003.3.4|issn=0081-6906}}</ref> version of the sum-product problem of [[György Elekes]] and [[Imre Z. Ruzsa]]. A consequence of their result is that any set with a small sumset (such as an [[arithmetic progression]]) has the lower bound on the product set

<math display=block>|A\cdot A|=\Omega\left(|A|^2\log^{-1}|A|\right).</math>

Xu and Zhou proved<ref name=":6">{{citation
 | last1 = Xu | first1 = Max Wenqiang
 | last2 = Zhou | first2 = Yunkun
 | article-number =  10
 | arxiv = 2201.00104
 | doi = 10.19086/da
 | journal = Discrete Analysis
 | mr = 4620309
 | pages = 1–31
 | title = On product sets of arithmetic progressions
 | year = 2023}}</ref> more strongly that

<math display=block>|A\cdot A|=\Omega\left(|A|^2\log^{1-2\log 2-o(1)}|A|\right)</math>

for any dense subset <math>A</math> of an arithmetic progression in integers, which is sharp up to the <math>o(1)</math> in the exponent.

As an example for the corresponding ''few products, many sums'' version of the problem, the set <math>B=\{2,4,8,\dots,2^n\}</math> satisfies <math>|B\cdot B=2|B|-1</math> but has many sums: <math>|B+B| = \tbinom{|B|+1}{2}</math>. This bound comes from considering the [[Binary number|binary]] representation of a number. The set <math>B</math> is an example of  a [[geometric progression]].

For a [[Random number generation|random]] set of <math>n</math> numbers, both the product set and the sumset have cardinality <math>\tbinom{n+1}{2}</math>; that is, [[with high probability]], neither the sumset nor the product set generates repeated elements.

=== Sharpness of the conjecture ===
[[Paul Erdős|Erdős]] and [[Endre Szemerédi|Szemerédi]] give an example of a sufficiently [[Smooth number|smooth]] set of integers <math>A</math> with the bound<ref name=":0" />

<math display="block">\max\{|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\} \leq |A|^{2} e^{-\frac{c \log|A|}{\log\log|A|} }.</math>

This shows that the <math>o(1)</math> term in the conjecture is necessary.

=== Extremal cases ===
Often studied are the extreme cases of the hypothesis:
* '''few sums, many product''' ('''FSMP'''): if  <math>|A+A\ll|A|</math>, then <math>|A\cdot A|\ge|A|^{2-o(1)}</math>,<ref name=":2" /> and
* '''few products, many sums''' ('''FPMS'''): if <math>|A\cdot A|\ll|A|</math>, then <math>|A+A|\ge|A|^{2-o(1)}</math>.<ref>{{citation|last1=Murphy|first1=Brendan|last2=Rudnev|first2=Misha|last3=Shkredov|first3=Ilya|last4=Shteinikov|first4=Yuri|date=2019|title=On the few products, many sums problem|journal=Journal de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux|volume=31|issue=3|pages=573–602|doi=10.5802/jtnb.1095|arxiv=1712.00410|s2cid=119665080}}</ref>

=== Complex numbers ===
Proof techniques involving only the [[Szemerédi–Trotter theorem]] extend automatically to the complex numbers, since the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem holds over <math>\C^2</math> by a theorem of Tóth.<ref>{{citation|last=Tóth|first=Csaba D.|date=February 2015|title=The Szemerédi-Trotter theorem in the complex plane|journal=Combinatorica|volume=35|issue=1|pages=95–126|doi=10.1007/s00493-014-2686-2|issn=0209-9683|arxiv=math/0305283|s2cid=13237229}}</ref> Konyagin and Rudnev<ref>{{citation|last1=Konyagin|first1=Sergei V.|last2=Rudnev|first2=Misha|date=January 2013|title=On New Sum-Product–Type Estimates|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|volume=27|issue=2|pages=973–990|doi=10.1137/120886418|issn=0895-4801|arxiv=1111.4977|s2cid=207065775}}</ref> matched the exponent of <math>\tfrac43</math> over the complex numbers. The results with exponents of the form <math>\tfrac43+c</math> have not been matched over the complex numbers.

== Over finite fields ==
The sum-product problem is particularly well studied over [[finite field]]s. Motivated by the finite field [[Kakeya conjecture]], [[Thomas Wolff|Wolff]] conjectured that when <math>p</math> is a (large) prime, for every subset <math>A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p</math>, the inequality <math>\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|)\ge\min(p,|A|^{1+\varepsilon})</math> holds for an absolute constant <math>\varepsilon>0</math>. This conjecture had also been formulated in the 1990s by [[Avi Wigderson|Wigderson]],<ref>{{citation|last=Trevisan|first=Luca|date=2009-06-20|title=Guest column: additive combinatorics and theoretical computer science|journal=ACM SIGACT News|volume=40|issue=2|pages=50–66|doi=10.1145/1556154.1556170|s2cid=12566158|issn=0163-5700}}</ref> motivated by [[randomness extractor]]s.

Note that the sum-product problem cannot hold in finite fields unconditionally due to the following example:

'''Example:''' Let <math>\mathbb{F}</math> be a finite field and take <math>A=\mathbb{F}</math>. Then since <math>\mathbb{F}</math> is closed under addition and multiplication, <math>A+A=A\cdot A=\mathbb{F}</math>, and so <math>|A+A|=|A\cdot A|=|A|</math>. This pathological example extends to taking <math>A</math> to be any sub-field of the field in question.

Qualitatively, the sum-product problem has been solved over finite fields:

'''Theorem''' (Bourgain, Katz, Tao (2004)):<ref name=":3">{{citation |last1=Bourgain |first1=Jean |last2=Katz |first2=Nets |last3=Tao |first3=Terence |date=2004-02-01 |title=A sum-product estimate in finite fields, and applications |journal=Geometric and Functional Analysis |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=27–57 |arxiv=math/0301343 |doi=10.1007/s00039-004-0451-1 |issn=1016-443X |s2cid=14097626}}</ref> Let <math>p</math> be prime and let <math>A\subset\mathbb{F}_p</math> with <math>p^{\delta}<|A|<p^{1-\delta}</math> for some <math>0<\delta<1</math>. Then <math>\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|)\ge c_\delta|A|^{1+\varepsilon}</math> for some <math>\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\delta)>0</math>.

[[Jean Bourgain|Bourgain]], [[Nets Hawk Katz|Katz]], and [[Terence Tao|Tao]] extended this theorem to arbitrary fields. Informally, the following theorem says that if a sufficiently large set does not grow under either addition or multiplication, then it is mostly contained in a dilate of a sub-field.

'''Theorem''' (Bourgain, Katz, Tao (2004)):<ref name=":3" /> Let <math>A</math> be a subset of a finite field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> so that <math>|A|>|\mathbb{F}|^{\delta}</math> for some <math>0<\delta<1</math>, and suppose that <math>|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\le K|A|</math>. Then there exists a sub-field <math>G\subset \mathbb{F}</math> with <math>|G|\le K^{C_\delta}|A|</math>, an element <math>x\in\mathbb{F}\setminus\{0\}</math>, and a set <math>X\subset \mathbb{F}</math> with <math>|X|\le K^{C_\delta}</math> so that <math>A\subseteq xG\cup X</math>.

They suggest that the constant <math>C_\delta</math> may be independent of <math>\delta</math>.

Quantitative results towards the finite field sum-product problem in <math>\mathbb{F}</math> typically fall into two categories: when <math>A\subset\mathbb{F}</math> is small or large with respect to the [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of <math>\mathbb{F}</math>. This is because different types of techniques are used in each setting.

=== Small sets ===
In this regime, let <math>\mathbb{F}</math> be a field of characteristic <math>p</math>. Note that the field is not always finite. When this is the case, and the characteristic of <math>\mathbb{F}</math> is zero, then the <math>p</math>-constraint is omitted.

In fields with non-prime order, the <math>p</math>-constraint on <math>A\subset\mathbb{F}</math> can be replaced with the assumption that <math>A</math> does not have too large an intersection with any subfield. The best work in this direction is due to Li and Roche-Newton<ref>{{citation|last1=Li|first1=Liangpan|last2=Roche-Newton|first2=Oliver|date=January 2011|title=An improved sum-product estimate for general finite fields|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|volume=25|issue=3|pages=1285–1296|doi=10.1137/110823122|issn=0895-4801|arxiv=1101.5348|s2cid=7024012}}</ref> attaining an exponent of <math>\delta=\tfrac{1}{19}</math> in the notation of the above table.

=== Large sets ===
When <math>\mathbb{F}\subset\mathbb{F}_p</math> for <math>p</math> prime, the sum-product problem is considered resolved due to the following result of Garaev:<ref>{{citation|last=Garaev|first=M. Z.|date=2008-04-14|title=The sum-product estimate for large subsets of prime fields|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|volume=136|issue=8|pages=2735–2739|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-08-09386-6|issn=0002-9939|arxiv=0706.0702|s2cid=16064726}}</ref>

'''Theorem''' (Garaev (2007)): Let <math>A\subset\mathbb{F}_p</math>. Then
<math display=block>\max(|A+A|,|A\cdot A|\gg\min(p^{1/2}|A|^{1/2},|A|^2p^{-1/2}).</math>

This is optimal in the range <math>|A|\ge p^{2/3}</math>.

This result was extended to finite fields of non-prime order by Vinh<ref>{{citation|last=Vinh|first=Le Anh|date=November 2011|title=The Szemerédi–Trotter type theorem and the sum-product estimate in finite fields|journal=[[European Journal of Combinatorics]]|volume=32|issue=8|pages=1177–1181|doi=10.1016/j.ejc.2011.06.008|doi-access=free|issn=0195-6698|arxiv=0711.4427}}</ref> in 2011.

== Variants and generalizations ==

=== Other combinations of operators ===
Bourgain and [[Mei-Chu Chang|Chang]] proved unconditional growth for sets <math>A\subset\Z</math>, as long as one considers enough sums or products:

'''Theorem''' (Bourgain, Chang (2003)):<ref>{{citation |last1=Bourgain |first1=Jean |last2=Chang |first2=Mei-Chu |date=2003-11-25 |title=On the size of <math>k</math>-fold sum and product sets of integers |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=473–497 |arxiv=math/0309055 |bibcode=2003math......9055B |doi=10.1090/s0894-0347-03-00446-6 |issn=0894-0347 |s2cid=15154515}}</ref> Let <math>b\in\N</math>. Then there exists <math>k\in\N</math> so that for all <math>A\subset\Z</math>, one has
<math display=block>
\begin{align}\max\left(|kA|,|A^{(k)}|\right)
&=\max\left(|A+A+\cdots+A|,|A\cdot A\cdot\cdots\cdot A|\right)\\
&\ge|A|^b.
\end{align}
</math>

In many works, addition and multiplication are combined in one expression. With the motto ''addition and multiplication cannot coexist,'' one expects that any non-trivial combination of addition and multiplication of a set should guarantee growth. Note that in finite settings, or in fields with non-trivial subfields, such a statement requires further constraints.

Sets of interest include (results for <math>A\subset\R</math>):

*<math>A\cdot A+A</math>: Stevens and Warren<ref name=":5">{{citation
| last1=Stevens | first1=Sophie
| last2=Warren | first2=Audie
| title=On sum sets of convex functions
| date=2022
| arxiv=2102.05446
| journal=Electronic Journal of Combinatorics
| volume=29
| issue=2
| article-number=P2.18
| doi=10.37236/10852 | doi-access=free}}</ref> show that
<math display=block>|A\cdot A+A|\gg|A|^{\tfrac{3}{2}+\tfrac{3}{170}-o(1)}.</math>
*<math>A\cdot(A+A)</math>: Murphy, Roche-Newton and Shkredov<ref>{{citation|last1=Murphy|first1=Brendan|last2=Roche-Newton|first2=Oliver|last3=Shkredov|first3=Ilya D.|date=January 2017|title=Variations on the Sum-Product Problem II|url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/17M112316X|journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=31|issue=3|pages=1878–1894|doi=10.1137/17M112316X|issn=0895-4801|arxiv=1703.09549|s2cid=207074281}}</ref> show that
<math display=block>\left|A\cdot(A+A)\right|\gg|A|^{\tfrac{3}{2}+\tfrac{5}{242}-o(1)}.</math>
*<math>A\cdot(A+1)</math>: Stevens and Warren<ref name=":5" /> show that 
<math display=block>\left|A\cdot(A+1)\right|\gg|A|^{\tfrac{49}{38}-o(1)}.</math>
*<math>(A\cdot A)+(A\cdot A)</math>: Stevens and Rudnev<ref name=":4" /> show that
<math display=block>\left|(A\cdot A)+(A\cdot A)\right|\gg|A|^{\tfrac{127}{80}-o(1)}.</math>
